Question 2.1 - Data frame (file_name, content) and denoising

# Q2.1
unzip("news.zip", exdir = "news", overwrite = TRUE)
files <- list.files("news", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)
files <- files[!grepl("(__MACOSX|/\\.)", files)]

news_df <- tibble(
  file_name = basename(files),
  content   = map_chr(files, ~ paste(readLines(.x, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8"), collapse = " "))
)
cat("Documents loaded:", nrow(news_df), "\n")
## Documents loaded: 10
head(news_df |> mutate(content = substr(content, 1, 120)))
## # A tibble: 6 × 2
##   file_name   content                                                           
##   <chr>       <chr>                                                             
## 1 news_1.txt  Eskom former official, service provider appear in court Tuesday, …
## 2 news_10.txt Wet, cold weather expected to continue in Western Cape Monday, Ju…
## 3 news_2.txt  Gauteng Education commits to implementing Mayibuye Primary School…
## 4 news_3.txt  New Labour Minister charts the way forward  Tuesday, July 9, 2024…
## 5 news_4.txt  Police recue two kidnapped victims in Benoni Tuesday, July 9, 202…
## 6 news_5.txt  President Ramaphosa sends condolences to deceased SANDF members T…

The following denoising techniques were applied: transliteration of non-ASCII characters, lower-casing, removal of URLs, e-mail addresses, HTML tags, numbers and punctuation, whitespace normalisation, removal of empty and duplicate documents, stop-word removal (standard and domain-specific news words), removal of tokens shorter than three characters, and lemmatisation.

# Q2.1
clean_text <- function(x) {
  x |>
    iconv(to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT", sub = " ") |>
    tolower() |>
    str_replace_all("http\\S+|www\\.\\S+|\\S+@\\S+", " ") |>
    str_replace_all("<[^>]+>", " ") |>
    str_replace_all("[0-9]+", " ") |>
    str_replace_all("[[:punct:]]", " ") |>
    str_squish()
}

news_df <- news_df |>
  mutate(clean = clean_text(content)) |>
  filter(nchar(clean) > 50) |>
  distinct(clean, .keep_all = TRUE)

custom_stop <- tibble(word = c("said","say","mr","mrs","also","will","year","new","one","two",
                               "can","just","like","get","told","people"))
tokens <- news_df |>
  unnest_tokens(word, clean) |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") |>
  anti_join(custom_stop, by = "word") |>
  filter(nchar(word) > 2) |>
  mutate(word = lemmatize_words(word))

cat("Documents after cleaning:", n_distinct(tokens$file_name), " | Tokens:", nrow(tokens), "\n")
## Documents after cleaning: 10  | Tokens: 1926
tokens |> count(word, sort = TRUE) |> head(15)

Question 2.2 - LDA: top n topics and top k words

Number of topics

# Q2.2
dtm <- tokens |> count(file_name, word) |> cast_dtm(file_name, word, n)
dtm <- removeSparseTerms(dtm, 0.99)
dtm <- dtm[row_sums(dtm) > 0, ]
dtm
## <<DocumentTermMatrix (documents: 10, terms: 866)>>
## Non-/sparse entries: 1177/7483
## Sparsity           : 86%
## Maximal term length: 19
## Weighting          : term frequency (tf)
# Q2.2
ks <- 2:8
perp <- sapply(ks, function(k) perplexity(LDA(dtm, k = k, control = list(seed = 1234))))
tune <- tibble(topics = ks, perplexity = perp)
ggplot(tune, aes(topics, perplexity)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") + geom_point(size = 3, colour = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = ks) +
  labs(title = "Figure 2.1 - Perplexity by number of topics",
       x = "Number of topics (k)", y = "Perplexity (lower is better)") +
  theme_minimal()

tune

## 2      3       257.
## 3      4       205.
## 4      5       177.
## 5      6       160.
## 6      7       134.
## 7      8       118.

LDA model

# Q2.2
n_topics <- 5
k_words  <- 10

lda <- LDA(dtm, k = n_topics, method = "Gibbs",
           control = list(seed = 1234, iter = 1000, burnin = 200))

beta  <- tidy(lda, matrix = "beta")
gamma <- tidy(lda, matrix = "gamma")

top_terms <- beta |> group_by(topic) |> slice_max(beta, n = k_words, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(topic, desc(beta)) |> ungroup()

Top k words per topic

# Q2.2
top_terms |>
  group_by(topic) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number(), word = paste0(term, " (", round(beta, 3), ")")) |>

  select(rank, topic, word) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = topic, values_from = word, names_prefix = "Topic ") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Top words per topic with beta (word probability) in brackets")

Findings

The corpus consists of 10 South African news articles. After denoising, 1926 meaningful tokens remained, and the most frequent terms were department (34), government (29), service (28), public (26), invoice (18), which reflects the dominant subject matter of the collection.

Perplexity was calculated for models with 2 to 8 topics; the lowest perplexity was obtained at k = 8 (118.4). A 5-topic model was retained because, for a small corpus of 10 articles, it balances statistical fit with topics that remain distinct and interpretable.

The word distribution per topic is summarised below:

  • Topic 1 is characterised by service, public, invoice, day, department. Its top 10 words carry 27.4% of the topic’s probability mass, the topic accounts for 25.0% of the corpus on average and it is the dominant topic in 3 article(s).
  • Topic 2 is characterised by government, coalition, administration, include, role. Its top 10 words carry 20.8% of the topic’s probability mass, the topic accounts for 16.3% of the corpus on average and it is the dominant topic in 1 article(s).
  • Topic 3 is characterised by department, priority, ensure, unemployment, continue. Its top 10 words carry 18.0% of the topic’s probability mass, the topic accounts for 16.5% of the corpus on average and it is the dominant topic in 1 article(s).
  • Topic 4 is characterised by eskom, report, south, school, action. Its top 10 words carry 19.4% of the topic’s probability mass, the topic accounts for 19.3% of the corpus on average and it is the dominant topic in 2 article(s).
  • Topic 5 is characterised by police, expect, cape, cold, weather. Its top 10 words carry 15.0% of the topic’s probability mass, the topic accounts for 22.9% of the corpus on average and it is the dominant topic in 3 article(s).

Topic 1 is the most prevalent theme in the collection (25.0% average share), which indicates that it is the subject most frequently reported on in these articles.

Question 2.3 - Visualisations

Visualisation 1 - Top words per topic

# Q2.3
top_terms |>
  mutate(term = reorder_within(term, beta, topic)) |>
  ggplot(aes(beta, term, fill = factor(topic))) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ topic, scales = "free", labeller = label_both) +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  labs(title = "Top 10 Words per LDA Topic", x = "Beta (probability of word within topic)", y = "Term")

Visualisation 2 - Word cloud per topic

# Q2.3
par(mfrow = c(2, ceiling(n_topics / 2)), mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0))
for (t in seq_len(n_topics)) {
  d <- beta |> filter(topic == t) |> slice_max(beta, n = 40, with_ties = FALSE)
  wordcloud(d$term, d$beta, scale = c(3, 0.5), colors = brewer.pal(8, "Dark2"), random.order = FALSE)
  title(paste("Topic", t))
}

Visualisation 3 - Word-topic heat map

# Q2.3
top_terms |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(topic), reorder(term, beta), fill = beta)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Word-Topic Probability Heat Map", x = "Topic", y = "Term", fill = "Beta")

Findings

The bar charts and word clouds show the highest-probability word in each topic: Topic 1 - service (beta = 0.050); Topic 2 - government (beta = 0.058); Topic 3 - department (beta = 0.045); Topic 4 - eskom (beta = 0.031); Topic 5 - police (beta = 0.023). The larger the bar or the word in the cloud, the more strongly that word defines the topic.

The heat map shows that 2 word(s) (department, south) rank among the top words of more than one topic, which indicates some overlap between these themes, while the remaining words are specific to a single topic and make the topics clearly distinguishable.
